Hacknet is a fun and intriguing hacking puzzle game. Unlike many other games that are controlled by command line, such as TIS-100, Hacknet does not feature any actual programming. This is simultaneously kind of accurate to what a lot of "hacking" is, and also makes the game more accessible.

Individual puzzles will have you hacking into one or more computers to achieve some goal, often as contracts. A simple request might be to delete a file from a computer. But there might be a variety of obstacles in your way: You might not be given the location of the computer, and have to find its IP address elsewhere. The computer might be heavily protected. The file itself might be hidden.

As the complexity of the puzzles ratchets up, so do the stories behind them. The main storyline involves a security company developing dangerous hacking software. A particularly memorable one-off mission, should you choose to accept it, tasks you with euthanizing a terminally ill patient.

Way back when, there was this cool game called Uplink. It was a hacking simulator. You bounce your connection off of hacked machines, hide your steps, steal data. It was sort of close to how real hacking works, but it was just different enough and directionless to a point that it was kind of overwhelming. It was a hard game.

Hacknet is something of an Uplink-inspired indie game. Its terms and tools are much closer to the real world. It's also quite a bit more straightforward. It's paced well enough, with a mixture of contract-type hacking jobs, and some narrative missions that lead to a story conclusion. The mission objectives are clear enough that I never failed for incompletion. However, I found some missions were either offered before I had the tools to complete them, or without ever having the tools and forcing me to abort the contract to continue.

To complete missions, you have to combine your tools with your knowledge. An early mission involves a counter-hack. Someone has stolen a file. You need to get on their server, find the file, and delete it. The tools will get you into the server, but you're on your own for finding the file. Part of it is knowing where to look, and part is knowing what you're looking for. If you think you've got it right, you send a reply to the customer, and get a "contract successful" email. If you didn't, the game will stop you from replying with a "mission incomplete" screen.

On most servers, there's no particular danger to browsing around and screwing up. However, some will start tracing your location. If you let the trace catch you, you're thrown into a minigame in which you have to reset your own IP address by hacking your ISP. It's on a short timer, so you move from the intense countdown of the trace, to an even more intense countdown before you're disconnected. It'd make for some really cool moments, if it were a little better explained the first time it happens. I didn't have a firm grasp on what to do, so I kind of just sat there until I lost. Not great.

But the highs of the game are rather high. It's fun to try to solve the puzzles getting into servers, doing it under the timer of the trace, and getting out. Some parts are less developed than others, and the appeal might be limited to people who have an interest in computer security, but it's a good game for a weekend. Or a day, it really only took me 5 something hours to complete.

TL;DR - Get the game. Now

This is, perhaps, one of the stranger games I've ever played, but I'm totally glad that I did.  As you begin cracking into systems you end up meeting with some pretty enjoyable dilemmas and puzzles.  Even after cracking every system in the vanilla game, with 3 unique and interesting stories to follow for great replay value, I still find myself coming back to this game just to play through again and again. 

At first, I wasn't sure if I would enjoy a "terminal-based" game, starting with very little knowledge beyond old DoS systems, but the game walks you through it in a comfortable pace that's easy to learn with a little bit of practice and a little bit of /help.  The story is immersive and the UI is actually kind of impressive, especially for leaving up in a domain control room at work! ;)
This was the first game that, while still definitely a little bit of a fantasy world, actually looked and felt a little bit like real hacking.

Immersive, realistic gameplay; exciting storylines; strong characters (especially given text basis); and challenging. Hacknet is a fun game that I'm sad to say I've completed. The whole game is a puzzle, and you'll be diving into files to figure out the mystery of Bit, your first contact. While Hacknet is obviously geared toward the more technically-apt, the game feels like a sci-fi mystery, where you collect information and move quickly to uncover the storyline. Full of hilarlious text, mind-flexing challenges, and satisfying accomplishment, Hacknet was one of my favorite games this year.

Besides the game itself, Hacknet lends itself to being great in lots of different situations. It's fun to pick up and prod at for ten minutes, or to turn up the music, pull out a notepad, and really get crackin' at the puzzle. I found myself taking notes, more as I came closer to the end of the game, and going over everything I'd done in a particular puzzle to try and figure it out.

This game is likely the best hacking simulation that will ever be, and one of the best text-heavy games of its generation. Computer people will love its implementations of the kernel, and others will find themselves comfortable with the UI elements and basic commands to use in the game.

Problem-solve and explore - this game is full to the brim with storyline and unique easter eggs for any player that dives in to the Hacknet.

Review for Hacknet + Labyrinth DLC:
A game that offers a unique challenge and is a rewarding experience, but won't appeal to everyone - only geeks need apply!
A variety of hacking scenarios are presented that require some thought, but ultimately become somewhat repetitive - a greater variety of hacking tools and strategies would help here. The plot is just sufficient to keep things moving along, but could benefit from some stronger writing. The ending is low-key, but ultimately satisfying. I'd recommend this as a novel gaming experience.
The Labyrinth DLC adds some new tools and challenges, and is well worth getting.
